studies.title: Four Oaths And A Question
studies.meaning: Four oaths are sworn and then, where the claim should stand, a question arrives instead: is there in that an oath for one who has understanding. The sworn statement is never supplied, and the classical commentators supply it from the lines that follow. On the oaths themselves they record a range. The ten nights are read most often as the first ten of the pilgrimage month and sometimes as the last ten of the fasting month; the even and the odd as days of the rites, as every created pair set against the single Creator, or as the prayers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The pilgrimage season long predated the mission: tribes converged on Mecca in named months when fighting stopped, markets opened on the approach roads, and the whole year was counted toward that arrival. An audience hearing oaths sworn on a daybreak and on ten nights did not need them explained. They were the calendar the city ran on.

keyTerms.note: From a root of bursting open, the same word used of a spring breaking through ground. It names the splitting of the darkness rather than the sun, so the oath is on a moment, not a light.
A single unpaired thing, the word also used for a bowstring. It occurs only here in the Quran, and the readings run from the odd-numbered days of the rites to God Himself as the one without a second.
The root means to fence off or forbid. Intelligence is named by what it holds a person back from, so the question asks after a mind that restrains rather than one that merely reasons.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in Mecca was counted in nights rather than days, and a debt or a journey was fixed by how many had passed. Caravans left at first light to get the climb done before the heat. In the sacred months the roads filled: tribes who would otherwise raid each other travelled the same track, camped within sight of one another, and traded. The year had a shape, and everyone stood inside it.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah changes its rhyme more than once. The first five lines all close on the same consonant; the section that follows closes mostly on another; and by the final lines it has shifted again. Among the short chapters that is unusual, and each shift falls at the point where the subject changes, so the ear is told where the sections are.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reason is addressed as a moral faculty rather than an analytical one. The question does not ask whether the hearer can follow an argument; it asks whether there is anyone present whose mind restrains him. That reframes the whole set of oaths. They are not evidence for a proposition to be examined, but a set of familiar things placed in front of someone to see whether he will be moved by them at all.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other candidate for the ten nights its own surah, a single night worth more than a thousand months.
Names the pilgrimage months as known and fixed, the calendar the oaths here assume.
Swears by the departing night and the brightening morning, the same pair of moments in another early surah.

studies.applyIt: Be awake once this week for the twenty minutes before sunrise, outdoors if you can manage it. Do not fill them. Watch the point where shapes separate from the dark and things become distinguishable again. The surah swears by that moment, and it is hard to understand why until you have sat through one.

studies.title: Cities Built To Last
studies.meaning: Three powers are named, and each is identified by what it built. Aad is given with pillars and a claim that nothing like it was made in the land. Thamud is named by an action: they cut the rock in the valley. Pharaoh is given a title built from stakes, and the commentators read those as the pegs of an immense encampment, as his buildings, or as an instrument he used on people. What the three share is not yet their sin. It is that each is known by the thing meant to outlast it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The northern caravan route out of Mecca ran past rock-cut facades still standing in the cliffs, and Egypt's monuments were known to any trader who had gone that far. The argument is built on what the audience could go and look at. Classical commentators note that two of the three peoples were Arabian and remembered locally, while the third was foreign and known by report.

keyTerms.note: A plural for supporting columns, used equally of stone pillars and of the poles that hold a large tent. The readings split accordingly, between a city of architecture and a tribe famous for the height of its tents.
The root is one of cutting across something, used of traversing a country as well as of carving. It presents the shaping of rock as a kind of travel driven into stone.

Pegs driven into the ground to hold something down. Attached to a ruler it suggests an army's encampment or the solidity of his works, and the commentators keep both alongside a harsher third reading.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravans going north camped in stages, and one of those stages lay among tombs carved into cliff faces by people long gone, their doorways and columns still sharp. Drivers passed them every season. Meanwhile a tent's standing was read from its poles: a tall tent meant a chief, guests, and meat. Both kinds of building, the carved and the pitched, meant the same thing to the people who made them.
studies.didYouKnow: The name given to Aad here appears only once in the entire Quran, and the classical commentators cannot agree what it refers to. Some read it as a city, some as the tribe itself, some as an ancestor whose name the tribe carried. The Arabic grammar permits all three, and the sources set the options side by side without deciding.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The evidence offered is architecture, which is the most durable thing a civilisation makes and the thing it makes precisely in order to be remembered by. Each of the three built exactly what a people builds when it does not expect to end. The passage lets the buildings stand and removes the builders, so the monument that was meant to prove permanence ends up recording its absence.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same carving of houses out of mountains and names it among the favours given to Thamud.
Says the dwellings of both peoples were left plainly visible, evidence deliberately preserved for later travellers.
Questions Aad about building monuments on every high place and taking fortresses as though they would remain.

studies.applyIt: Find the oldest building you regularly walk past and look for the date on it, or ask who put it up. Most of the time nobody nearby knows. Notice how short the distance is between building something to be remembered by and being the anonymous person who built it.

studies.title: When He Calls It Honour
studies.meaning: The three named powers are gathered into a single relative clause with a single charge: they overstepped in the lands and multiplied ruin there. The punishment arrives as a verb of pouring, and what is poured is a whip. Then the surah turns without warning to one man's private reasoning. Given ease, he concludes that his Lord has honoured him. The classical commentators fasten on the verb: both the giving and the withholding are called a testing, so the man has read the examination as though it were the result.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca's wealth had grown fast on the caravan trade, and standing in the city tracked what a man could spend and who owed him. The surah moves from three vanished empires straight to the ordinary arithmetic of a prosperous merchant sitting in the audience, with no transition marked. Classical sources report no particular occasion and read the two halves as one continuous argument about how prosperity gets interpreted.

keyTerms.note: The root describes water rising past its bank and running where it should not. It makes excess a spilling over a limit rather than a decision, which is why the word attaches so readily to power.

A noun for a place of ambush overlooking a road. The only other use of this root in the Quran puts the fire itself in that position, so both times the image is a fixed point on a route that has to be travelled.

A verb of assaying, used of putting metal or a person to proof. The passage applies it to the comfortable case and the hard one alike, so neither condition reports anything about the person's standing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both images in this passage come off the road. Raiders waited at the narrow places where a track squeezed between rock, and caravan masters paid for guides who knew which defiles were watched that season. The whip belonged to the same world: drovers used one on the animals, overseers on people. A merchant hearing these lines pictured a pass he had ridden through with his heart up, not a courtroom.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing God as lying in wait occurs twice in the Quran from the same root. In the other place it is the fire that is described that way, waiting on the road. The image is identical in both, a position held above a route, and the two uses sit only a few surahs apart in the final part of the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prosperity is cut loose from approval, and the cut is made with one verb. If being given much and being given little are both trials, then neither can be read backwards as a verdict, and the whole apparatus by which people rank themselves collapses. The passage does not say the comfortable man is wicked. It says his conclusion does not follow, which is a narrower and more unsettling claim.

crossReferences.why: States the principle plainly, that both hardship and good are sent as a trial rather than a judgement.
Asks whether extended wealth and children are God hastening good for them, and answers no.
Quotes the same misreading, a man saying a favour was given him on account of his own knowledge.

studies.applyIt: The next time something goes well for you, catch the sentence that forms in your head about what it means about you. It arrives very fast and it usually contains the word deserve. You do not have to argue with it. Just notice that you produced it before you had any information.

studies.title: You Do Not Honour The Orphan
studies.meaning: A single word of refusal cuts the previous line off, and the correction that follows is not theological. It is an audit of behaviour, four items long, and the address changes from a man in the third person to a crowd in the second. You do not honour the orphan. You do not urge the feeding of the poor. You devour the inheritance, taking everything. You love wealth with a love the Arabic calls abundant. The commentators note that the second charge is not a failure to give but a failure to press anyone else to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Before Islam an estate in Mecca generally passed to those able to defend it, so a child who lost a father often lost the property in the same week and had no court to appeal to. Guardianship and control of the inheritance usually fell to the same relative. The surah names that arrangement rather than any individual, and the classical sources record no specific occasion for the lines.

keyTerms.note: A mutual form of pressing someone on. The charge concerns the absence of any pressure within the group toward feeding the poor, which puts the fault in the society rather than in one purse.
The estate considered as a thing handed down, and this is its only occurrence in the Quran. Consuming it is therefore eating what was meant to travel forward to someone else.
A verbal noun of scraping everything together and leaving no remainder. It turns the eating from appetite into method: the fault named is not excess but the absence of anything left over.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food in Mecca moved through clans. A man ate because his kin fed him, and public generosity was performed at gatherings where it could be counted and recited about afterwards. That system worked well for anyone inside it. A person with no clan, and a child whose protector had died, fell straight through it, and could go hungry within sight of a feast without anybody present feeling implicated.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for inheritance appears only once in the whole Quran, although the Book speaks about estates and heirs at length elsewhere using other words from the same root. Two of the four charges also close on intensive verbal nouns of the same shape, so the final pair arrives as a matched sound as well as a matched accusation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A mistake about God is answered with a list of social failures, and the surah never explains the connection. That silence is the point. Belief about what prosperity means and behaviour toward the people prosperity passed over are treated as one subject, so closely joined that no argument is needed to get from one to the other. The second charge widens it further: indifference is placed alongside taking.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly the same two failures, repelling the orphan and not urging the feeding of the poor, as evidence of denial.
Addresses the consuming of an orphan's property directly, naming the swapping of good for bad.
Pairs failure to believe with failure to urge feeding the poor as a single verdict on a life.

studies.applyIt: This week, instead of only giving something yourself, ask one other person to join you in it. A colleague, a sibling, a neighbour. The second charge in this list is not about your money at all; it is about whether anyone around you has ever heard you raise the subject.

studies.title: If Only I Had Sent Ahead
studies.meaning: Two lines repeat a word immediately after itself, which Arabic uses for an action that keeps going: the earth pounded, pounding after pounding, and the ranks arriving row upon row. Classical commentators are careful with the line about the Lord coming, reading it as His command or His decision arriving rather than attributing movement to Him. Then a man remembers, and the text says at once that remembering will not help him now. His sentence is a single regret, and it names no sin. He wishes he had sent something on ahead for his life.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people who treated a day of accounting as a figure of speech. Every verb in the scene is passive or impersonal: the earth is levelled, the fire is brought forward, the ranks are simply there. Nothing in the sequence is arranged by anyone present, which is the opposite of how the audience experienced authority in their own city. The classical sources report no occasion for these lines.

keyTerms.note: The word doubled means the flattening keeps going. The verb is used of beating a mound of earth level, so the ground is not shattered in an instant but worked down by repetition.
The same doubling for a different picture. This word is used of lines drawn up for battle and of lines standing in prayer, so what arrives is ordered rather than chaotic.
A verb of putting something ahead of you, used in trade of forwarding goods before a journey. The regret is shaped as a failure of provisioning rather than as a confession.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long-distance travel was managed by sending things ahead. Provisions went forward to a staging point with an earlier party, or a trader forwarded goods with a convoy leaving before his own. A man who arrived at a stage with nothing waiting for him was in serious difficulty, and everybody who had made the Syria run understood that arithmetic. The regret in this passage borrows that exact picture.
studies.didYouKnow: The regret calls the coming existence my life, not the one that has just ended. The Quran uses that reversal elsewhere, saying plainly that the home of the hereafter is the life, if only they knew. Here the correction is put in the mouth of the man himself, who arrives at the vocabulary at the moment it stops being useful to him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Memory is shown working perfectly and arriving too late, which is a sharper picture than forgetting. The man is not confused about anything by this point; he simply cannot act on what he now sees. The passage also locates the whole problem in sequence rather than in knowledge. Everything he would need was available earlier, and the only thing missing was that nothing was sent to where he is now standing.

crossReferences.why: Turns the same verb forward instead of backward, asking each soul to look at what it has sent on for tomorrow.
States directly what the man here works out too late, that the coming home is the actual life.
Describes the same day as the one on which a person looks at what his own hands sent ahead.

studies.applyIt: Do one thing today whose whole benefit lands on somebody else, at a time when you will not be there to see it. Set up a standing payment, plant something, write the letter that gets read later. The point is not the size of it. The point is practising the direction, which is the only thing the man in this passage got wrong.

studies.title: Return, Pleased And Pleasing
studies.meaning: Two ayat of shackles and punishment end, and without transition the address changes to a single soul, in the feminine, and the tone changes completely. It is called settled, at rest, and told to return. Two words describe the state of that return, one active and one passive: pleased, and found pleasing. Then two invitations rather than one, and the order matters. Enter among My servants comes before enter My garden.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah that opens with oaths by the dawn and ten nights. It then runs through destroyed peoples and a diagnosis of how people read wealth and poverty. No set occasion is reported for these ayat. Where they sit is the point. The surah's harshest lines come immediately before, and the shift from that scene to this address happens with no joining word.

keyTerms.note: From a verb for ground that has stopped shifting and for a heart that has stopped moving about. It names steadiness reached rather than calm felt, so the description is of a state that arrived and stayed.
Two forms of one root, active and passive, side by side. The pairing makes the satisfaction mutual and is one of the tightest constructions in the Quran, four syllables carrying both directions.

An imperative of returning rather than of arriving, which implies the soul is going somewhere it came from. Early scholars stress that word: the destination is described as home rather than as a new place.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic addresses a soul in the feminine. This passage speaks to one directly, by name. That is how a person would call to someone across a courtyard. The words for returning belonged to travel as well. A caravan came back. A herd came back. For people who spent months away, the word for a homecoming was one of the warmest in the language.
studies.didYouKnow: God speaks in the first person in the last two lines, and the possessive is used twice: My servants, My garden. The Quran more often describes paradise without that pronoun. The effect is that the place is named by its owner rather than by its contents, and nothing at all is said here about what is in it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The invitation to enter among the servants comes before entering the garden. That puts company ahead of place, which is a specific claim about what the reward is made of. The doubled word for satisfaction does something similar. It is not enough for the soul to be content; the passage says the pleasure runs both ways. And the whole address arrives with no transition from the description of punishment.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same root for a settled heart and names what settles it, which this passage assumes.
Names another condition of the same soul, so the two passages describe stages rather than different things.
Repeats the same two-way satisfaction as a description of a group rather than as an address to one soul.

studies.applyIt: Notice what your soul is currently unsettled about. Name it in one sentence, without solving it. Then ask what would have to be true for that particular thing to stop moving. Often the answer is not a change in the situation but a decision you have been deferring, and this passage describes the state on the other side of it.
studies.explainEasier: After lines about punishment, God speaks to one calm soul. He tells it to come back to him, happy with him and pleasing to him. Then he says: come in among my servants, and come into my garden.
